gendered_labor.assessment: Complementary/parallel-spheres model is the dominant scholarly framing. Men's public/martial role (warfare, tribute) was ideologically framed as directly dependent on and equally essential to women's domestic-ritual labor (weaving, food preparation, home-based ritual practice, childbirth reframed as a form of "warrior" service/capture). Louise Burkhart's work specifically demonstrated men's battlefield success was ideologically tied to women's home-front ritual performance.

sources.citation: Burkhart, Louise M. Work on Aztec gender ideology and complementarity (specific monograph title not pinned in this research pass; commonly associated with The Slippery Earth: Nahua-Christian Moral Dialogue in Sixteenth-Century Mexico, University of Arizona Press, 1989).
Dodds Pennock, Caroline. Bonds of Blood: Gender, Lifecycle and Sacrifice in Aztec Culture. Basingstoke: Palgrave Macmillan, 2008.
sources.author: Caroline Dodds Pennock

political_inequality.assessment: State rulership (tlatoani) and the highest political-military offices (cihuacoatl office, military command) were exclusively male in the documented record. No confirmed cases of female tlatoque in Tenochtitlan itself. Important terminological precision: "Cihuacoatl" names both a female earth/childbirth-associated deity AND the second-highest office in Tenochtitlan's government (created under tlatoani Itzcoatl, r. 1427-1440) — an office held by men (most famously Tlacaelel, for roughly six decades). These are two distinct, name-sharing entities, not a contradiction to resolve away; the dualistic Nahua cosmological logic behind naming a powerful male office after a goddess is itself a documented point of scholarly interest.

sources.citation: Wikipedia, "Cihuacoatl (position)," cross-corroborated by general Mexica political-history sourcing.

legal_economic_status.assessment: Susan Kellogg, Law and the Transformation of Aztec Culture, 1500-1700, University of Oklahoma Press, 1995, based on 73 property lawsuits before the Real Audiencia (1536-1700) plus pre-contact-era wills: pre-Hispanic Mexica women held real, documented property and inheritance rights — inheritance passed through both male and female lines, women could and did will property (including favoring female heirs in some surviving wills). Kellogg's key dynamic finding: colonial Spanish law subsequently ERODED these rights, shifting households from bilateral/multifamily kinship structures toward Spanish-style nuclear patrilineal families and increasing women's legal subordination over the 16th-17th centuries — i.e. the pre-conquest baseline was LESS patriarchal in property terms than the colonial trajectory that followed.

sources.citation: Kellogg, Susan. Law and the Transformation of Aztec Culture, 1500-1700. Norman: University of Oklahoma Press, 1995.
sources.author: Susan Kellogg

household_authority.assessment: Complementary-parallel model again dominant: women held real domestic-sphere authority (household management, ritual, economic production via weaving/marketplace activity) described by specialists as "equally essential," not merely subordinate-but-tolerated.

sources.citation: Dodds Pennock, Caroline. Bonds of Blood: Gender, Lifecycle and Sacrifice in Aztec Culture. Palgrave Macmillan, 2008.
sources.author: Caroline Dodds Pennock

gendered_legal_restrictions.assessment: Documented gender-restricted religious offices existed: girls could be dedicated in infancy to become cihuatlamacazqui (female priests/priestesses), serving through their teens, typically only "several years" before leaving to marry — contrasted with male priests who could serve for life. Priestesses conducted rituals for female deities and taught girls at calmecac/telpochcalli schools, but were explicitly barred from officiating human sacrifice at major festivals honoring their own goddesses, and could not attain the highest priestly offices, reserved for men.

sources.citation: General secondary sourcing on cihuatlamacazqui (female priesthood) drawing on Florentine Codex material (Heather on History, "Aztec priestesses"; Zoe Saadia, "cihuatlamacazqui").

ideological_patriarchy.assessment: DISPUTED. [COMPLEMENTARITY/PARALLELISM — Susan Kellogg; Louise Burkhart; Inga Clendinnen (1990s); Caroline Dodds Pennock]: Mexica gender ideology structured around "parallel but distinct spheres," male and female roles ideologically framed as equally necessary to cosmic/social order — described by multiple secondary sources as probably the dominant paradigm in current specialist studies of Mesoamerican gender relations. [HIERARCHY/PATRIARCHY-CRITIQUE — general critical commentary, e.g. Alice Evans's essays "Getting Real about Aztec Patriarchy" and "Aztec Patriarchy: Women's Work and Men's War"]: argues the complementarity framing risks minimizing real, structural patriarchal features — militaristic, male-dominated state religion and rulership, warfare-centered ideology instrumentalizing women's reproductive/ritual labor in service of a male-controlled tribute-and-conquest system; Pete Sigal, The Flower and the Scorpion: Sexuality and Ritual in Early Nahua Culture, Duke University Press, 2011, is cited as complicating the complementarity picture further. Both camps agree on the underlying facts (real property/inheritance rights, restricted-but-real religious roles, no access to top political/military office, an ideology valorizing female domestic/reproductive labor as cosmically necessary) and disagree on how much weight to give "equally necessary but categorically separate and subordinate in state power" relative to "genuine complementary parity."

sources.citation: Dodds Pennock, Caroline. Bonds of Blood: Gender, Lifecycle and Sacrifice in Aztec Culture. Palgrave Macmillan, 2008.
sources.author: Caroline Dodds Pennock

sources.citation: Sigal, Pete. The Flower and the Scorpion: Sexuality and Ritual in Early Nahua Culture. Durham, NC: Duke University Press, 2011.
sources.author: Pete Sigal

dimensions.notes: Required does_not_demonstrate: neither the documented property/inheritance rights nor the restricted-priestess-role evidence, alone, settles a whole-society verdict of "complementary parity" or "patriarchal hierarchy" — both camps above are working from the same underlying documented facts and disagree on their relative weight, not on the facts themselves.
